stem.en: The headings of the columns of a table are called:

explanation.en: Column headings are captions; row headings are stubs.

stem.en: The row headings of a table are called:

explanation.en: Stubs are the designations of the rows, written in the left-most column.

stem.en: Textual presentation of data is most suitable when:

options.en: The quantity of data is small
We want to compare many groups at a glance
We want to draw a graph

explanation.en: When data are few, they can be described in a paragraph. With large data, text becomes hard to follow.

stem.en: Which part of a table tells the reader where the data were taken from?

explanation.en: The source note at the bottom names the origin of the data, such as the Census of India.

solution.en: The source note at the bottom names the origin of the data, such as the Census of India.

stem.en: A table showing the literacy rate of Karnataka for 1991, 2001 and 2011 uses which classification?

explanation.en: The data are arranged by census years, i.e. by time.

A bar diagram that shows the parts of a total (like expenditure on food, rent and education) within each bar is a:

explanation.en: A component bar diagram divides each bar into parts, each showing a component of the total.

stem.en: To compare the exports and imports of India for five years side by side, the most suitable diagram is a:

explanation.en: A multiple bar diagram places two or more bars side by side for each year, making comparison easy.

Bar diagrams are called one-dimensional diagrams because:

options.en: Only the length (height) of the bars matters; the width does not
They are drawn on one axis

explanation.en: In a bar diagram all bars have the same width; the value is shown only by the height.

stem.en: A histogram is drawn for:

explanation.en: A histogram shows a grouped frequency distribution with continuous classes; bars touch each other.

stem.en: In a histogram there are no gaps between bars because:

explanation.en: The upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next, so the rectangles are drawn next to each other.

stem.en: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining:

options.en: The mid-points of the tops of the rectangles of a histogram
The class limits on the x-axis
The upper-right corners of the rectangles

explanation.en: The mid-points of the tops (class mark, frequency) are joined by straight lines, and the polygon is closed at both ends on the x-axis.

stem.en: In a histogram with unequal class widths, the heights of the rectangles should be based on:

explanation.en: In a histogram the area of each rectangle shows the frequency. With unequal widths, heights must be adjusted to frequency per unit width.

solution.en: In a histogram the area of each rectangle shows the frequency.
With unequal widths, heights must be adjusted to frequency per unit width.

stem.en: A smooth freehand curve drawn through the points of a frequency polygon is called a:

explanation.en: Smoothing the frequency polygon gives a frequency curve.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): A histogram is a two-dimensional diagram.
Reason (R): In a histogram both the width (class interval) and height of the rectangles matter, since area represents frequency.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Unlike bar diagrams, area (width × height) shows the frequency in a histogram, so it is two-dimensional. R explains A.

stem.en: An ogive is also called a:

explanation.en: An ogive plots cumulative frequencies against class limits.

stem.en: The point where the "less than" ogive and the "more than" ogive cut each other gives the:

explanation.en: At the intersection, half the observations are below and half above that value, which is the median.

stem.en: In a "less than" ogive, cumulative frequencies are plotted against:

explanation.en: For "less than" we count values below each upper limit; for "more than" we use lower limits.

stem.en: For classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, 40–50 with frequencies 3, 5, 7, 5, the "less than 40" cumulative frequency is:

explanation.en: 3 + 5 + 7 = 15 observations are less than 40.

stem.en: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph) shows:

options.en: How a variable changes over time

explanation.en: Time is taken on the x-axis and the value of the variable on the y-axis; the points are joined by lines.

stem.en: For the same data (frequencies 3, 5, 7, 5 for 10–20 … 40–50), the "more than or equal to 30" cumulative frequency is:

explanation.en: Values 30 and above fall in 30–40 and 40–50: 7 + 5 = 12.

A frequency distribution has classes 0–10 (f = 15), 10–30 (f = 40) and 30–35 (f = 12). In a correctly drawn histogram, the tallest rectangle is for the class:

explanation.en: Class widths are unequal, so heights are frequency densities: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5, 40 ÷ 20 = 2 and 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4. The class 30–35 is tallest even though its frequency is smallest.

solution.en: Class widths are unequal, so heights are frequency densities: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5, 40 ÷ 20 = 2 and 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4.
The class 30–35 is tallest even though its frequency is smallest.

stem.en:
Which of the following statements are correct?
(A) The less than ogive rises from left to right.
(B) The more than ogive is plotted against upper class limits.
(C) The less than and more than ogives intersect at the median.
(D) A histogram is a one-dimensional diagram.

explanation.en: The more than ogive uses lower class limits (B is wrong), and a histogram is two-dimensional because area shows frequency (D is wrong). A and C are correct.
